role: Source of bw_new: the benchmark with the new read kernel (part A)
purpose: bandwidth.c is a benchmark: each thread runs one kernel (read, write or copy) in whole passes over its own buffer for a minimum time, and `main` prints one rate in GB/s per timed interval. This version holds the new read kernel: 16 NEON loads per 256 B and no arithmetic.

main_flow.step: `main` sets the defaults and reads the arguments. Part A passes `--threads 120 --cpus 0-119 --bytes 256M --kernel NAME --reps 3 --min-ms 500` [Ref5].
`main` checks the values. The buffer size must be a multiple of 256 B.
`main` creates the barrier for all benchmark threads plus itself and starts the threads.
Each thread binds itself to its CPU, maps its buffer and writes the whole buffer once. This is not timed.
For each selected kernel and each repetition, each thread runs one warm-up pass and then waits at the barrier.
`main` waits at the same barrier. When all benchmark threads and `main` wait there, the barrier releases them, and the threads start the timed interval.

Each thread reads the clock and runs whole passes of the kernel. With the 256 MiB buffers of part A it reads the clock after each pass. It stops after the first pass that ends 0.5 s or more after its start.
Each thread stores its bytes and its elapsed time. Then it waits at the barrier for the other threads and for `main`.
`main` computes the rate of the interval from the results of all threads and prints one row.
After the last repetition of a kernel `main` prints the `best` row and writes the output.
After the last kernel the threads end, and `main` ends the process.

behavior_notes: **Which definitions are compiled.** The first `k_read`, `k_write` and `k_copy` are in lines 143 to 165. The first `pass` is in lines 388 to 414. Both blocks are text inside C comments (lines 136 to 166 and lines 381 to 415). They are not under a preprocessor condition. The compiler reads only the definitions of lines 184, 213, 239 and 418 [Ref8].

**Proof from the binary.** The loop of `k_read` in bw_new has 11 instructions: 8 `ldp` loads, 1 `add` of 256 to the address, 1 `cmp` and 1 branch. After the loop comes `ret`. The function has no add of data, and it returns no value. That is the definition of line 184. The old definition adds every word to a sum: `k_read` in bw_old has 8 vector `add` instructions per 128 B and returns the sum [Ref1].

**Preprocessor conditions.** Only two are active: `#if defined(__aarch64__)` in line 294 and `#if HAVE_ASM_KERNELS` in line 430. Both are true on CRB. Proof: bw_new holds `k_asmread`, `k_asmwrite` and `k_asmcopy` [Ref1].
**Build.** gcc 14.2.0 on CRB with the flags `-O3 -march=native -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns -pthread -Wall -Wextra -std=gnu11`. The same command built bw_old and bw_new [Ref1] [Ref4].

**Is this file the source of bw_new?** A build from a file with the sha256 of this file gave a bw_new with the sha256 of the binary that the rerun used. The proof has three steps. The build record of 18:32:18 UTC on 2026-11-13 lists the sha256 of this file (f1985072...) for bandwidth.c and fd7c14df... for bw_new [Ref3]. ra.sh runs bw_new only when it has the sha256 fd7c14df... [Ref5]. The three result folders of part A record that value for bw_new [Ref9]. The binary bw_new is not in the local folders. Its sha256 is known only from records such as these. One limit: the earlier build record of 18:12:22 UTC lists another sha256 for bandwidth.c (c1406e02...), with the same sha256 of bw_new and the same listings [Ref1]. So the source text changed between the two builds, and the binary did not change. The run of 18:12:22 had the mode `all`: it is the run that timed the test of 2026-11-13 [Ref1]. The run of 18:32:18 had the mode `probe`: it built the binaries and timed nothing [Ref3] [Ref4]. The two texts differ in comment lines only. An edit of 2026-11-13 18:32:07 UTC replaced 2 comment lines above `k_read` with the 5 comment lines 178 to 182 of the local text [Ref10]. With this edit reversed, the local text has the sha256 value of the earlier text (c1406e02...). No code line differs.

**What is timed.** The time from the clock read of line 471 to the last clock read of line 476. It holds the passes and the clock reads between them. Not timed: the start of the threads, the binding, the mapping and the first write of the buffer, the warm-up pass before every interval, and the waits at the barrier.

**Stop rule (whole-pass stop).** A thread tests the time only after a whole pass over its 256 MiB buffer. Every thread therefore ends at its own time, 0.5 s or more after its own start. A thread that has ended waits at the barrier and runs no kernel while the other threads end their last pass. During that time fewer than 120 threads run the kernel.

**Rate.** `aggregate_GBps` = sum of the bytes of all threads / longest elapsed time of any thread / 1e9. With the kernel `read` every thread counts 268,435,456 bytes (the buffer size) per whole pass. A copy kernel counts 2 times that. The value is at most the sum of the thread rates. Example: the first interval of bw_new with the kernel `read` in session 1 shows 330.59 GB/s. In the same row, 120 times the mean thread rate (2.84 GB/s) is about 340.8 GB/s [Ref6].

**Few passes per interval.** The example row of the note **Rate** counts 178,241,142,784 bytes. That is 664 passes for 120 threads, or about 5.5 passes per thread on average. 16 of the 18 intervals of bw_new with the kernel `read` in the three sessions of part A count exactly this number of bytes. In these 16 rows the rate differs only through `elapsed_s`, the longest thread time [Ref6].

**Threads and buffers in part A.** 120 threads. Thread `i` is bound to CPU `i` (0 to 119). Each thread maps its own 256 MiB buffer, asks for huge pages, and writes the whole buffer once after it is bound. In a process with the kernel `copy` or `asmcopy` each thread maps and writes a second buffer of the same size. The huge page setting of CRB was `[always]` at the start of each session of part A [Ref9]. The source comment of lines 129 to 130 says that on a machine with this setting a buffer gets 2 MiB pages also without a request from the program. Insufficient data: whether the buffers of part A lay on huge pages. This file prints no page state. The field AnonHugePages in the file /proc/PID/smaps of a running bw_new process would resolve it.

**The thread of `main`.** This file does not bind it to a CPU. ra.sh runs the process under `taskset -c 0-119`, so Linux may run `main` on any of these CPUs [Ref5]. During a timed interval `main` waits at the barrier.

**Order inside one process of part A.** One kernel only. For each of the 3 intervals: one warm-up pass, the barrier, then the timed passes. The file holds no sleep call. A thread starts the warm-up pass of the next interval as soon as the second barrier releases it. ra.sh sets the order of the processes [Ref5].

**Difference to the old source, 1 of 6: the read kernel.** Old: portable C, every 8-byte word is added to one of 16 running sums, and the function returns the total. New: 16 NEON loads per 256 B, no arithmetic, no return value. Machine code on CRB: the old loop reads 128 B per loop pass, so 256 B need 2 loop passes. These 2 loop passes hold 32 instructions: 8 `ldp`, 16 vector `add`, and 8 more for the address, the counter, the compare and the branch. The new loop reads 256 B in 1 loop pass of 11 instructions: 8 `ldp`, 1 `add`, 1 `cmp` and 1 branch [Ref1].

**Difference 2 of 6: the result of the read kernel.** After its loop the old `k_read` adds its 16 sums to one value, once per pass. The old `pass` stored that value into the variable `sink` on the stack of the thread, once per pass. The new code has neither step [Ref2].

**Difference 3 of 6: `k_write`.** Old: a plain C loop that gcc compiled to a loop of SVE store instructions. New: 16 NEON stores per 256 B, compiled to 8 `stp`. This changes the kernel `write`. In a process with the kernel `read` it changes only the code of the first write of the buffer, which is not timed. Both versions leave the same content: every 8-byte word holds `v` [Ref1] [Ref2].
**Difference 4 of 6: `k_copy`.** Old: a plain C loop that gcc compiled to a loop of SVE load and store instructions. New: 8 `ldp`, then 8 `stp`, per 256 B. This changes the kernel `copy` only [Ref1].

**Difference 5 of 6: the place of the code in the binary.** The three `asm` kernels have the same source text and the same instructions in both binaries, at other addresses. Example: `k_asmread` starts at the address 0x1b40 in bw_new and at 0x1c88 in bw_old [Ref1]. Part A runs `asmread` with both binaries, so its output compares the same loop in the two binaries [Ref5].

**Difference 6 of 6: lines that cannot change a rate.** Line 10 (the include), line 492 (the usage text) and the two comments that hold the old text. Apart from the differences 1 to 4 and these lines, both files hold the same text: `worker` apart from `sink`, the stop rule, `alloc_buf`, `pin_cpu`, `now_s` and the rate computation in `main` [Ref2].

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
one pass of go.sh through part A, part L and part C.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).

the whole-chip read test of 2026-11-17. It was run after the memory speed of CRB was lowered from 8000 MT/s to 7200 MT/s (MT/s = million transfers per second, the unit of memory speed). Part A, part L and part C are parts of it. Only part A runs bw_old and bw_new.
the driver script of the rerun. It calls ra.sh once per session.
the stop rule of bandwidth.c: after the minimum time (0.5 s here) each thread finishes the pass over its buffer that it is in. The threads stop at different times.
one of the six inner loops of this benchmark: read, write, copy, asmread, asmwrite, asmcopy. It never means the Linux kernel.
one run of a kernel over the whole buffer of one thread. The function `pass` runs one.
one run of the loop body of a kernel. The new read kernel reads 256 B in one loop pass.
B = byte. MiB = 2^20 bytes = 1,048,576 bytes. GB = 1e9 bytes.
the rate that this file prints for one interval: the bytes of all threads, divided by the longest elapsed time of any thread. Unit GB/s.
the bytes of one thread in one interval, divided by the elapsed time of that thread. Unit GB/s.
the 64-bit instruction set of Arm processors. gcc defines the macro `__aarch64__` when it compiles for it.
the vector instructions of AArch64 with registers of 16 B.
a C function that maps to a machine instruction. `vld1q_u64` loads 16 B into a vector. `vst1q_u64` stores 16 B from a vector.
Scalable Vector Extension: a second set of vector instructions of Arm processors. The listing shows its registers as z and p registers.
the Arm instructions "load pair" and "store pair". With q registers one instruction moves 32 B: two registers of 16 B.
names of the vector registers of AArch64. q5 and v5 are the same register of 16 B. d5 is its low 8 bytes.
the C compiler that built the binaries: version 14.2.0 on CRB [Ref1].
a gcc extension that puts assembly text into a C function. The lists after the text tell the compiler which values the text reads, changes and overwrites.
the text that the tool objdump printed from a binary: one line per machine instruction. The listings of bw_old and bw_new are in the build record [Ref1].
the file probe.txt that run_kernels.sh wrote at a build: compiler, flags, sha256 values and listings [Ref1].
run_kernels.sh is the script of 2026-11-13 that built bw_old and bw_new [Ref4]. ra.sh is the script that runs part A of the rerun [Ref5].
a line such as `#if`. The compiler reads the lines up to `#else` or `#endif` only when the condition is true.
an object of the thread library (`pthread_barrier_t`). A thread that calls `pthread_barrier_wait` waits until a fixed number of threads have called it. Then all of them continue.
Linux assigns a physical page to new memory at the first access to that page. This event is a page fault. Here the first access is a write.
a memory page of 2 MiB. Linux can use such pages for normal memory by itself (transparent huge pages, THP).
to restrict a thread to one CPU.
a Linux tool that starts a command with a fixed set of allowed CPUs.
the C library function that fills memory with one byte value.
a pass that runs before the timed interval. Its bytes and its time are not counted.
the number that a process returns when it ends. 0 means success.
a checksum. Two files with the same sha256 have the same content.

functions.name: now_s
functions.what: Reads the Linux clock `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` in seconds. `worker` calls it at the start of an interval and, in the whole-chip test, after each pass.

functions.name: parse_bytes
functions.what: Turns a size such as `256M` into bytes. The suffix k, m or g multiplies by 2^10, 2^20 or 2^30.

functions.name: parse_cpus
functions.what: Turns a CPU list such as `0-119` into the array `cfg.cpus`.

functions.name: pin_cpu
functions.what: Binds the calling thread to one CPU with `sched_setaffinity`.

functions.name: alloc_buf
functions.what: Maps one buffer, aligned to 2 MiB, and asks Linux for huge pages. Linux assigns no physical page here.

functions.name: k_read (old text inside a comment)
functions.what: Text of the old read kernel with 16 running sums. It is inside a comment. The compiler does not read it.

functions.name: k_write (old text inside a comment)
functions.what: Text of the old write kernel. It is inside a comment. The compiler does not read it.

functions.name: k_copy (old text inside a comment)
functions.what: Text of the old copy kernel. It is inside a comment. The compiler does not read it.

functions.name: k_read
functions.what: New read kernel. One loop pass loads 256 B with 16 NEON loads (8 `ldp` instructions on CRB) and drops the values.

functions.name: k_write
functions.what: New write kernel: 256 B of stores per loop pass. It also writes every buffer once before any timing.

functions.name: k_copy
functions.what: New copy kernel: one loop pass loads 256 B and then stores 256 B.

functions.name: k_asmread
functions.what: Kernel `asmread`: hand-written loop with 8 `ldp` loads per 256 B. The old source holds the same text.

functions.name: k_asmwrite
functions.what: Kernel `asmwrite`: hand-written loop with 8 `stp` stores per 256 B. The old source holds the same text.

functions.name: k_asmcopy
functions.what: Kernel `asmcopy`: hand-written loop with 8 `ldp` and 8 `stp` per 256 B. The old source holds the same text.

functions.name: pass (old text inside a comment)
functions.what: Text of the old `pass` with the `sink` parameter. It is inside a comment. The compiler does not read it.

functions.name: pass
functions.what: Runs the selected kernel once over the buffer. Returns the bytes moved: the buffer size, or 2 times the buffer size for a copy kernel.

functions.name: worker
functions.what: One benchmark thread. It binds itself, maps and writes its buffer. Per interval it runs a warm-up pass and the timed passes.

functions.name: usage
functions.what: Prints the argument list and ends the program with exit status 2.

functions.name: main
functions.what: Reads the arguments, starts the threads, starts each interval at the barrier, computes the rates and prints the rows.
